title: ERP-WMS stock reconciliation note - July (cutoff timing only)
content: July ERP vs WMS stock gap of £980k was put down to cutoff timing only: WMS posts receipts 1-3 days after ERP records the inbound PO. No status-mapping or item-level analysis was done and no prevention step was agreed, so the gap came back. To be replaced by a fuller write-up and archived.

title: UK-Vietnam FTA: preferential origin rules for garments
content: UK-Vietnam FTA preferential duty on garments (HS 61/62) needs originating status: the garment must be substantially transformed in Vietnam AND at least 65% of its ex-works value must originate in Vietnam or the UK (regional value content). Fabric from China is non-originating, so cut-and-sew in Vietnam from Chinese fabric normally does NOT qualify (fabric is typically 40-60% of cost) and pays full duty. To qualify: (1) buy Vietnamese-made or UK fabric, or weave/knit the fabric in Vietnam from yarn; or (2) raise Vietnamese value added so non-originating Chinese content stays under 35%. Evidence: a certificate of origin issued per shipment by the Vietnamese Ministry of Industry and Trade (or its authorised chamber), with commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, fabric mill supplier declarations and the factory cost breakdown proving the 65% content. Keep records 4 years.

title: Carrier tender scorecard: criteria, weights and disqualifying thresholds
content: Weight criteria by what has cost us most (damage and loss claims first, then delay and service failures), not by price alone. Recommended weights: on-time delivery 30%; damage and loss performance (claims rate and claim recovery) 25%; cost per shipment 20%; compliance and safety (insurance, operator licence) 10%; tracking and EDI visibility 10%; sustainability 5%. Score each criterion 1-5. Minimum thresholds that disqualify a bidder: on-time delivery below 90%; damage and loss rate above 1.0% of shipments; cargo liability cover below £100k per consignment; no live tracking or EDI feed; no current operator licence or safety accreditation. Review scores quarterly during the contract.

title: Returned goods and EPR rules: Germany, France, Netherlands
content: Germany (VerpackG, duty of care): register in LUCID and join a dual system before shipping packaging; usable returned goods must not be destroyed. Penalties up to £75k per breach plus sales ban. Reporting: annual data report to the Central Agency and quarterly volumes to the dual system. France (AGEC law): destroying unsold or returned non-food goods is banned, they must be reused, donated or recycled; EPR through Citeo (packaging) and Refashion (textiles); Triman recycling label required. Penalties up to £80k. Reporting: annual declaration of products placed on market and unsold-goods disposal. Netherlands: packaging EPR through Afvalfonds Verpakkingen; textile EPR scheme with producer registration; annual volume reporting. Penalties up to £65k. Strictest: France (destruction ban plus highest penalties). Likely conflicts for us: scrapping returned stock in France or Germany, and missing label or registration in each country.

title: Sourcing country disruption: warning signs, trigger points and contingencies
content: Watch list for our sourcing countries (China, Vietnam, India, Bangladesh, Turkey): export restrictions (India cotton or yarn export curbs), power shortages (rolling cuts or gas rationing in Bangladesh, northern Vietnam and southern China), political unrest (strikes, hartals or street protests near ports and industrial zones, mainly Bangladesh), typhoon season at Vietnamese ports, Turkey currency volatility. Recommended trigger points for action (any one): factory power cuts above 4 hours a day for 3 consecutive days; port or road blockade lasting over 48 hours; new export restriction covering our category; government travel advisory raised to essential travel only. Contingency when triggered: list open POs not yet shipped, bring shipments forward, air-freight the most urgent, move volume to alternate suppliers (Turkey, Portugal for short-lead items) and hold 2-3 weeks of buffer stock on best sellers. Review country risk quarterly.

title: Morocco vs Turkey nearshore sourcing comparison
content: Incentives: Morocco - EU association agreement (zero duty on originating goods), Tangier and Kenitra free zones with multi-year tax holidays, state training subsidies; Turkey - UK-Turkey FTA (zero duty on originating goods), regional investment incentives. Labour: Morocco has a smaller skilled garment workforce but wages 30-40% below Turkey; Turkey has a large skilled workforce but wages rising fast with inflation. Fabric: Morocco imports most fabric (Turkey, Spain, China), which can break origin rules; Turkey has integrated mills from yarn to fabric, best fabric availability. Risk: Morocco - stable politics, dirham managed against a EUR/USD basket so low currency risk; Turkey - lira volatile with high inflation, regional proximity to Syria and Iraq, earthquake exposure. Tailoring: Morocco is better for tailored suits and jackets (established tailoring lines for EU brands); Turkey is better for knitwear, denim and fast reorders. Lead time: Morocco 8-12 weeks and consistent; Turkey 6-10 weeks but variable. Cost premium vs Asia: Morocco 15-20%, Turkey 10-15%.

title: Co-development IP protection clauses
content: Recommended: Buyer owns all derivative IP; supplier retains pre-existing IP. Escrow for know-how transfer. Non-compete 2-year post-termination.

title: Supplier lead-time reduction programme: structure, retailer results, supplier needs
content: Structure (6-9 months): 1) baseline the order-to-ship lead time by step (fabric booking, cutting, sewing, QC, shipping booking), month 1; 2) quick wins live by month 3: remove approval waits, pre-position trims, release a rolling 12-week forecast; 3) process redesign months 3-6: line balancing, in-line QC, smaller batches, pilot on one line; 4) sustain: weekly lead-time KPI and quarterly review. Retailer results: peers cut lead time 15-25% (typically 18%); one cut 22% in 6 months for about £50k of consulting, saving about £200k a year (ROI 4:1). What the supplier needs from us: a rolling 12-week forecast accurate to +/-20%, a frozen firm-order window of 8 weeks, sample and approval turnaround under 5 days, early fabric and trim commitment, a shared KPI dashboard, a named buyer and QA owner, and joint workshops (sometimes shared training cost).

title: Supplier fraud red flags
content: Watch for: sudden large discounts below market; new bank details pre-first-order; fake certifications. Control: sanctions screening; trade finance verification; site audit before first PO.

title: 3PL integration EDI API comparison
content: EDI: 4-6 weeks setup; £5k per year; 2-4 hour latency. API: 2-3 weeks setup; £15k initial plus £10k per year; real-time. File transfer: 1 week; less than £2k; manual risk.

title: Recycled nylon abrasion test failures
content: Trial recycled-nylon fabric failed abrasion tests at 50k cycles vs 100k target. Root cause: lower fiber strength in recycled material. Solution: blend 20 percent virgin nylon with recycled to maintain performance. Cost impact: material cost up 3 percent; performance meets spec.

title: Technical finish performance gap lab to field
content: New durable water-repellent finish passes lab tests but fails in field after 5 washes. Lab conditions: controlled humidity; field conditions: real laundry; variable water hardness. Solution: revise test to include actual fabric weight and agitation cycle.

title: Seam strength and water resistance jacket failures
content: First sample technical jacket misses seam strength spec (50N vs 65N required) and water resistance. Construction issue: seam allowance too tight. Fix: increase allowance by 3mm; verify water resistance with revised construction.

title: Credit hold policy and customer payment terms
content: Credit hold policy: Customers more than 60 days overdue are placed on credit hold. Shipments paused until payment received or payment plan agreed. Legal review required before proceeding with recovery steps. Finance approval required for any hold release.

title: RFID and EAS tagging for shrink control
content: RFID tag and EAS (Electronic Article Surveillance) implementation reduces shrink by 30-40% when combined with layout optimization. Tagging cost: £0.15-£0.25 per unit. ROI: 2-3 months in high-shrink stores. Best practice: implement tags at receipt, use EAS gates at exit, combine with staff training.

title: Nearshore capacity commitments: how retailers structure priority-capacity deals
content: Typical structure: framework agreement with a committed minimum volume of about 60% of annual forecast (equal to 15-20% of the factory capacity, one dedicated line), the rest flexible; capacity reservation fee of 2-3% of committed value credited against orders; priority allocation in peak. Never commit above 70% of the low-case demand forecast or more than 30% of the supplier's capacity (dependency risk). Term 2-3 years. Clauses that protect us if demand drops: volume flexibility band of +/-20% on 8 weeks' notice, shortfall payment capped at 10% of committed value (take-or-pay), buy-back of finished goods and fabric bought against firm orders, rolling forecast that is non-binding beyond the frozen firm-order window, and termination for convenience on 90 days' notice.

title: Apparel supplier agreements: market norms and unusual terms
content: Normal in apparel: payment 30-60 days from goods receipt; liability capped at order value or 12 months of purchases, with product safety, death or injury, and IP claims uncapped; buyer owns designs and patterns, supplier keeps pre-existing know-how; force majeure excludes strikes, supplier financial failure and shipping delays; right to audit and a signed code of conduct; AQL inspection with right to reject. Unusual or red flags: payment terms over 90 days or payment before shipment; liability capped below order value or excluding product safety; supplier keeping IP in our designs or free to resell them; subcontracting without consent (main social-compliance risk); price changes after order confirmation; minimum volume commitments or exclusivity binding us; no audit right; auto-renewal beyond 12 months.

title: AMR fleet firmware update, rollback and safety re-validation runbook
content: Update: pilot on 2 robots for 48 hours, then roll out zone by zone with the fleet manager (about 30 minutes per zone). Keep the previous firmware image (4.6) on the fleet manager for 30 days. Rollback: stop dispatch to the zone, select the previous image and push it to the robots (about 15 minutes per robot, batches of 5); trigger it if more than 2 robot faults a day or localisation errors appear. Safety: any firmware change touching navigation or safety-rated lidar zones requires the HSE safety validation to be re-run (emergency stop, speed and separation monitoring, zone stop) before robots return to service; allow 2 days per zone. Peak: change freeze starts mid-November, so firmware changes must land by the first week of November, and not during peak trading weeks.
